sender: Gregory Voss, Senior Analyst, Regional Banks, Linwood Hart & Co.
subject: Regional Banks: FDIC final rule on brokered deposits published - deposit-cost math for 12 names; Buy list unchanged
body:
LINWOOD HART & CO. | U.S. Regional Banks | Regulatory Update

The FDIC final rule on brokered deposits was published in the Federal Register yesterday (Oct 14) and takes effect Jan 1, 2027.

What the rule does:
- It narrows the definition of a "deposit broker" for fintech and sweep-program placements. Placements where the partner does not have an exclusive relationship with the customer are treated as non-brokered.
- It keeps the well-capitalized exemption for the primary-purpose test but requires annual attestation filings.
- It sets a 90-day phase-in for reporting. Safe-harbor language for reciprocal deposit networks is unchanged.

Our math for the 12 banks in our coverage (all figures are our estimates):
- Median brokered and sweep-sourced deposits are 6.8% of total deposits. About 40% of that would be reclassified as non-brokered under the new definition.
- This frees up roughly 2-4 points of headroom under the brokered-deposit concentration limits that most boards use internally. It does not directly lower funding costs.
- Funding cost improvement is a second-order effect. If banks replace 25% of wholesale CDs with reclassified sweep balances, we calculate a 3-6bp benefit to net interest margin. That is under 1% of 2027 NII.

Names most affected: Calder Ridge Bancorp, Harmon Valley Financial and Stonehaven Trust each have more than 10% of deposits in sweep programs. We raise Harmon Valley's 2027 EPS by 2% to $3.41. Other estimates are unchanged.

Bottom line: This is helpful for compliance and liquidity planning but is not a catalyst for the group. We maintain our Buy list (Harmon Valley, Stonehaven, Fenwick Savings) and our view that credit and CRE are the real debates into 3Q prints.

Gregory Voss | Linwood Hart & Co. Equity Research

sender: Gideon Marchetti, Partner, International Trade Group, Fenmore & Tarr LLP
subject: Client alert: Commerce draft 'domestic production credit' for chip tariffs - comment window open to Nov 13; large buyers' commitment letters in docket
body:
Fenmore & Tarr LLP | International Trade | Client Alert

To: Larchmont Ridge Capital TMT team

What happened
On Oct 13 Commerce published a Federal Register notice seeking comment on a draft framework that would let importers credit semiconductor tariffs against verified U.S. fabrication, packaging and assembly. It would sit under the pending Section 232 semiconductor action. This is a request for comment, not a final rule. No tariff rate is set, and the rate will come from a separate presidential proclamation.

Proposed mechanics
- Credit would be calculated from the share of an importer's chip value that is verified as U.S.-fabricated or U.S.-packaged, subject to a cap.
- Companies could file "commitment letters" describing planned U.S. capacity. The docket already shows 31 filers.
- Verification would run through certification and audit, with details left to a later notice.

Open questions that will decide who benefits
1. Chips embedded in finished devices: does the credit apply at the chip level or the device level?
2. Wafers fabbed in Arizona but packaged in Taiwan: partial credit or none?
3. Custom silicon built by foundries or ODMs: does the designer or the importer of record claim the credit?

Companies named in the public docket (from their letters)
- Apple: cites its expanded U.S. supplier program and Houston server assembly. It is importer of record on finished iPhones, so the device-level question matters most.
- Nvidia: cites Arizona wafer production and U.S. rack assembly. Advanced packaging for Blackwell-class parts is still in Taiwan.
- Microsoft: cites Maia and Cobalt programs. Server imports run through ODMs, so the importer-of-record point applies.
- Amazon: cites Trainium and Graviton plus device lines (Echo, Kindle).
- Alphabet: cites TPU supply and Pixel devices.

Timeline
Comments are due Nov 13 and replies Nov 27. Commerce has said it aims to finalize the framework "by year-end." The timing of the proclamation is unclear, and there has been talk of a post-midterm window.

Our read
It is too early to size any company-level effect. Outcomes turn on definitions that have not been drafted. We can prepare a comment-tracker for the five names above if useful.

This alert is general information and not legal advice.

WHITCOMBE & LYLE SECURITIES | TELECOM REGULATORY UPDATE | Oct 15

FCC adopts final order on high-cost support reform

The Federal Communications Commission voted 3-2 yesterday to adopt a final order revising how high-cost Universal Service Fund support is distributed to rural local exchange carriers. The order resolves a proceeding opened in 2024.

Key provisions:
- Support for rate-of-return carriers moves to a model-based formula starting Jan 1, 2028, with a three-year glide path
- Carriers serving fewer than 5,000 access lines retain a legacy-support floor
- Broadband buildout obligations are raised to 100/20 Mbps for locations receiving support
- The quarterly contribution factor is expected to settle between 36% and 38% in 2027
- Reporting requirements are expanded, with annual certification by a corporate officer

Why it matters: Roughly 280 small carriers receive about $1.9bn annually in high-cost support. We estimate the order reduces support for the bottom quartile of carriers by 8-12% by 2030, while increasing it for carriers with larger, denser footprints. The contribution factor is a modest drag on consumer wireline and wireless bills.

Coverage implications:
- Consolidated rural carriers (CRC): neutral to slightly positive on model support
- Prairie Telecom Group (PTGP): negative; roughly 14% of revenue is legacy support
- Large wireless carriers: pay into the fund but see a broadly unchanged contribution

The order will be published in the Federal Register in coming weeks; petitions for reconsideration are due 30 days after publication.

Ratings unchanged across the telecom group.

Imogen Strand | Whitcombe & Lyle Securities

- Single payment amounts will be set at the median of winning bids rather than the maximum winning bid, a change CMS estimates will lower program spend by 3.8% over five years.
